# More than one predictor

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Multiple regression";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the word [pangolin]{.hl} comes from the Malay _pengguling_: "one who rolls up". Threatened pangolins curl into a ball of scales.

_Sources: Born Free Foundation; National Geographic_
:::

## Today

- Why one predictor is often [not enough]{.hl}
- Fitting and reading a model with [two]{.hl} continuous predictors
- What "[holding the other predictors constant]{.hl}" means
- Comparing predictors with [standardised]{.hl} coefficients
- Model fit: `R²` and [adjusted R²]{.hl}
- [Collinearity]{.hl}: when predictors overlap

## So far

- Lecture 4: one outcome, [one]{.hl} predictor: `y ~ x`
- Lecture 5: [centering]{.hl} and [standardising]{.hl} predictors
- And a warning: with the penguins, ignoring species [reversed]{.hl} a slope

. . .

Outcomes in linguistics rarely depend on one thing. Reaction times depend on word [frequency]{.hl}, word [length]{.hl}, the speaker, the task...

. . .

Today: [continuous]{.hl} predictors only. Categorical predictors (like species) come next week.

## The data {.smaller}

A simulated lexical decision experiment: one row per [word]{.hl}.

```{r}
set.seed(6)
words <- tibble(
  log_freq  = runif(400, 1, 6),                       # log10 frequency
  length    = pmin(pmax(round(11 - 1.1 * log_freq +   # in letters:
                              rnorm(400, 0, 1.6)), 2), 14),  # frequent words are shorter
  syllables = pmax(round(length / 3 + rnorm(400, 0, 0.35)), 1),
  rt        = 760 - 30 * log_freq + 14 * length + rnorm(400, 0, 45)
)
words
```

. . .

We [know]{.hl} the truth: frequent words are faster ([−30]{.hl} ms per log unit), longer words are slower ([+14]{.hl} ms per letter). Syllables have [no]{.hl} effect of their own.

## Two predictors, one outcome

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
bind_rows(
  transmute(words, x = log_freq, rt, predictor = "log10 frequency"),
  transmute(words, x = length,   rt, predictor = "Length (letters)")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.3, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

Frequent words are [faster]{.hl}. Long words are [slower]{.hl}. So far, so simple.

## The predictors are correlated {.smaller}

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
ggplot(words, aes(x = log_freq, y = length)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Length (letters)")
```

```{r}
cor(words$log_freq, words$length)
```

Frequent words tend to be [shorter]{.hl}. Each predictor carries part of the other's information.

## Two simple regressions

```{r}
coef(lm(rt ~ log_freq, data = words))
coef(lm(rt ~ length,   data = words))
```

. . .

Both slopes are [too big]{.hl} compared with the truth (−30 and +14).

. . .

On its own, [length]{.hl} also picks up the effect of frequency: long words are slow partly because they are [rare]{.hl}.

# One model, two predictors

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` pangolin scales are made of [keratin]{.hl}, like our fingernails. Scales and skin can make up about [25%]{.hl} of a pangolin's body weight.

_Sources: National Geographic; Born Free Foundation_
:::

## The equation

<div class="formula">y = b₀ + b₁ · x₁ + b₂ · x₂ + e</div>

- `b₀`: the predicted `y` when `x₁ = 0` and `x₂ = 0`
- `b₁`: the change in `y` when `x₁` increases by 1, [holding x₂ constant]{.hl}
- `b₂`: the change in `y` when `x₂` increases by 1, [holding x₁ constant]{.hl}

. . .

In R, add predictors with `+`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
lm(outcome ~ predictor1 + predictor2, data = ...)
```

## `lm()` with two predictors

```{r}
m <- lm(rt ~ log_freq + length, data = words)
coef(m)
```

. . .

- Each extra log unit of frequency: `r round(coef(m)["log_freq"], 1)` ms, [for words of the same length]{.hl}
- Each extra letter: `r round(coef(m)["length"], 1)` ms, [for words of the same frequency]{.hl}

. . .

Both are now close to the [true]{.hl} values. The multiple regression separated what the two predictors [share]{.hl}.

## Simple vs multiple {.smaller}

```{r, echo = FALSE}
slope <- function(f, term) coef(lm(f, data = words))[term]
tibble(
  predictor = c("log_freq", "length"),
  `true effect` = c(-30, 14),
  `simple regression` = c(slope(rt ~ log_freq, "log_freq"), slope(rt ~ length, "length")),
  `multiple regression` = c(coef(m)["log_freq"], coef(m)["length"])
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

. . .

With correlated predictors, a simple regression answers "what goes with `x`?". A multiple regression answers "what goes with `x`, [over and above]{.hl} the other predictors?".

## Holding the other predictor constant

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
grid_len <- crossing(length = 2:14, log_freq = c(2, 4, 6))
grid_len$fit <- predict(m, newdata = grid_len)

ggplot(words, aes(x = length, y = rt)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, colour = moss, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid_len, aes(y = fit, colour = factor(log_freq)), linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Length (letters)", y = "Reaction time (ms)", colour = "log10 frequency")
```

Predicted RTs from the model, for words of [three]{.hl} fixed frequencies. Each line has the [same]{.hl} slope: `r round(coef(m)["length"], 1)` ms per letter.

## Parallel lines

The lines are [parallel]{.hl} because our model says the effect of length is the [same]{.hl} at every frequency.

. . .

If the effect of length were [different]{.hl} for frequent and rare words, the lines would not be parallel. That is an [interaction]{.hl}: coming up in two weeks.

## A regression plane

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
plane <- crossing(log_freq = seq(1, 6, length.out = 80),
                  length   = seq(2, 14, length.out = 80))
plane$fit <- predict(m, newdata = plane)

ggplot(plane, aes(x = log_freq, y = length)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = fit)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = fit), colour = floor_col, alpha = 0.6, binwidth = 50) +
  geom_jitter(data = words, height = 0.2, colour = mist, alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = dim_col, high = hornbill) +
  labs(x = "log10 frequency", y = "Length (letters)", fill = "Predicted RT (ms)") +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"))
```

With two predictors, the model is a [plane]{.hl}, seen here from above. The contour lines are straight and evenly spaced: no curves, no interactions.

## `summary()` {.smaller}

```{r}
summary(m)
```

## `{broom}` and predictions {.smaller}

```{r}
tidy(m)[, 1:3]
```

. . .

Predict for words we choose, giving [every]{.hl} predictor a value:

```{r}
new_words <- tibble(log_freq = c(2, 5), length = c(9, 4))
predict(m, newdata = new_words)
```

. . .

A rare, long word versus a frequent, short one: a difference of about `r round(diff(rev(predict(m, newdata = new_words))))` ms.

# Standardised coefficients

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a pangolin's tongue can be up to [70 cm]{.hl} long. Pangolins have no teeth, and can eat up to 70 million insects a year, mostly ants and termites.

_Source: Born Free Foundation_
:::

## Which predictor matters more?

```{r}
coef(m)[-1]
```

. . .

[−29]{.hl} per log unit of frequency or [+15]{.hl} per letter? The units differ, so the numbers [cannot]{.hl} be compared directly.

. . .

From lecture 5: standardise the predictors, and every slope is "per [standard deviation]{.hl}".

## Standardising the predictors

```{r}
words <- words |>
  mutate(across(c(log_freq, length), \(x) as.numeric(scale(x)), .names = "{.col}_z"))

m_z <- lm(rt ~ log_freq_z + length_z, data = words)
coef(m_z)
```

. . .

- One SD more frequency: `r round(coef(m_z)["log_freq_z"])` ms
- One SD more length: `r round(coef(m_z)["length_z"])` ms

. . .

The intercept is now the predicted RT for a word of [average]{.hl} frequency and [average]{.hl} length.

## Same model, new numbers

```{r}
c(raw = glance(m)$r.squared, standardised = glance(m_z)$r.squared)
```

. . .

As in lecture 5: standardising changes what the coefficients [mean]{.hl}, never the [fit]{.hl}.

. . .

Standardised coefficients are useful to compare predictors [within]{.hl} a model. Raw coefficients are easier to [interpret]{.hl} ("ms per letter"): report the ones your reader needs.

# Model fit

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` Sunda pangolins climb trees to reach ant nests, holding on to branches with their [prehensile tail]{.hl}. During the day they sleep in tree hollows or burrows.

_Source: National Geographic_
:::

## `R²` with more predictors

```{r}
glance(lm(rt ~ log_freq,          data = words))$r.squared
glance(lm(rt ~ length,            data = words))$r.squared
glance(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length, data = words))$r.squared
```

. . .

Together, the predictors explain more than either alone, but [less]{.hl} than the sum of the two: they overlap.

## `R²` never goes down

Add a predictor of [pure noise]{.hl}:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
words <- words |> mutate(noise = rnorm(n()))

r2 <- c(glance(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length,         data = words))$r.squared,
        glance(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length + noise, data = words))$r.squared)
print(r2, digits = 6)
```

. . .

R² went [up]{.hl}, a tiny bit. Every new predictor fits some of the noise in the sample.

## Adjusted `R²`

Adjusted R² [penalises]{.hl} each extra predictor (`as.data.frame()` prints more digits):

```{r}
glance(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length,         data = words))[, 1:2] |> as.data.frame()
glance(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length + noise, data = words))[, 1:2] |> as.data.frame()
```

. . .

Use adjusted R² to compare models with [different numbers]{.hl} of predictors. A predictor that does not help lowers it.

## Checking assumptions

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
aug <- augment(m)
hist_df    <- transmute(aug, panel = "Histogram of residuals", x = .resid)
scatter_df <- transmute(aug, panel = "Residuals vs fitted", x = .fitted, y = .resid)

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(data = hist_df, aes(x = x), bins = 30, fill = orchid, colour = floor_col) +
  geom_hline(data = scatter_df[1, ], aes(yintercept = 0), colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = scatter_df, aes(x = x, y = y), colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

The same checks as lecture 4, on [one]{.hl} set of residuals for the whole model: roughly normal, constant spread.

# Collinearity

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the Sunda pangolin is [critically endangered]{.hl}. Pangolins are among the most trafficked mammals in the world; international commercial trade in them was banned in 2016.

_Source: National Geographic_
:::

## Overlapping predictors

Length in letters and length in syllables measure almost the [same]{.hl} thing:

```{r}
cor(words$length, words$syllables)
```

. . .

When two predictors are highly correlated, the model struggles to tell [which one]{.hl} does the work. This is __collinearity__.

## What collinearity does {.smaller}

```{r}
tidy(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length,             data = words))[, 1:3]
tidy(lm(rt ~ log_freq + length + syllables, data = words))[, 1:3]
```

. . .

- The [standard error]{.hl} of length grows: its estimate becomes less precise
- Syllables gets a coefficient, even though in our simulation it has [no]{.hl} effect
- The overall fit barely changes

## Measuring collinearity: VIF {.smaller}

The __variance inflation factor__: how well can a predictor be predicted from the [other]{.hl} predictors?

<div class="formula">VIF = 1 / (1 − R²ⱼ)</div>

```{r}
r2_len <- glance(lm(length ~ log_freq + syllables, data = words))$r.squared
1 / (1 - r2_len)          # length, with syllables in the model

r2_len2 <- glance(lm(length ~ log_freq, data = words))$r.squared
1 / (1 - r2_len2)         # length, without syllables
```

. . .

[1]{.hl} means no overlap. The higher the VIF, the more the standard error is [inflated]{.hl}. Common rules of thumb flag values above [5]{.hl} or [10]{.hl}.

## What to do about it

- Collinearity is a property of your [predictors]{.hl}, not an error in R
- Think about [theory]{.hl}: are the two predictors really different things?
- Keep the predictor that best answers your [research question]{.hl}, or combine them
- Never add predictors just because the data happen to contain them

# Your turn

## Exercises

With `penguins`, after `drop_na()` on the columns you use:

1. Predict `body_mass_g` from `flipper_length_mm` alone
2. Add `bill_length_mm` and `bill_depth_mm` as predictors
3. How did the flipper slope change? What is the adjusted R² of each model?
4. Standardise the three predictors. Which one goes with the largest change in body mass?
5. [Bonus]{.hl}: compute the VIF of `flipper_length_mm` in the model from 2

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
pengs <- drop_na(penguins, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)

m1 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = pengs)
m2 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm, data = pengs)

coef(m1)[2]; coef(m2)[2]
c(m1 = glance(m1)$adj.r.squared, m2 = glance(m2)$adj.r.squared)
```

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
pengs_z <- pengs |>
  mutate(across(c(flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm),
                \(x) as.numeric(scale(x))))

coef(lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm,
        data = pengs_z))[-1]

r2_flip <- glance(lm(flipper_length_mm ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm, data = pengs))$r.squared
1 / (1 - r2_flip)
```

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- `y ~ x1 + x2`: each slope is the effect of one predictor, [holding the others constant]{.hl}
- With correlated predictors, simple and multiple slopes [differ]{.hl}
- No interactions: the effect of one predictor is the [same]{.hl} at every value of the other (parallel lines)
- [Standardised]{.hl} coefficients compare predictors measured in different units
- `R²` always rises with more predictors; [adjusted R²]{.hl} does not
- [Collinearity]{.hl} inflates standard errors: check correlations and VIFs
:::
